segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at one of the oldest findings in memory research: the forgetting curve. In the 1880s, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus decided to study his own memory. He memorized lists of meaningless syllables, such as 'zub' and 'kef', and then tested himself after different delays.

What he found was striking. Within the first hour, he had forgotten about half of what he learned. After a day, only about a third remained. But the loss then slowed down: after a month, he still remembered a small but stable portion. When graphed, this decline forms a curve that drops steeply and then flattens.

Now, why does this matter? Ebbinghaus also discovered that review changes the curve. Each time he reviewed the material, the curve became less steep, which means that he forgot more slowly. This is the basis of spaced repetition: reviewing information at increasing intervals, such as after one day, three days, and a week, is far more efficient than studying everything in a single long session.
So, for your own studies, the lesson is clear. Review soon after learning, and then again just before you are about to forget.

To show that syllables are easy to remember

items.q: What happened to the curve each time Ebbinghaus reviewed the material?
items.explain: «the curve became less steep, which means that he forgot more slowly».

items.q: What would the professor most likely recommend to a student?

items.explain: Recomienda repasar a intervalos crecientes (repetición espaciada).
